novice.title: Novice Engineer
novice.blurb: Start here. What this tree covers and how the boxes work.

blocks.title: How this tree works
blocks.body:
This tree is laid out like a **Star Wars Galaxies** skill window, because that layout solved a real problem: it shows you the whole discipline at once, and it makes the order obvious without a syllabus.

Four columns, four tiers each:

- **Design** — deciding what to build and where the seams go
- **Code Craft** — writing code other people can change
- **Testing** — knowing whether it works, and continuing to know
- **Delivery** — getting it in front of users and keeping it there

Each box unlocks the one above it. Pass a module's quiz and the next tier opens. Finish the top of all four columns and **Master Engineer** unlocks.

> You can work the columns in any order, and you do not have to finish one before starting another. That is the point of the lattice: four parallel tracks, not one queue.

blocks.title: Authoring, not just reading

master.title: Master Engineer
master.blurb: All four disciplines, end to end.

blocks.title: What mastery actually looks like
blocks.body:
Having all four boxes filled does not mean knowing everything. It means the four disciplines stop being separate concerns and start informing each other:

- You **design** differently once you have operated the thing at 3am.
- You **write** differently once you have reviewed a hundred pull requests.
- You **test** differently once a test suite has lied to you.
- You **ship** differently once a deploy has gone wrong in a way no staging environment could have caught.

The honest version of mastery is a shorter feedback loop between those four, not a longer list of facts.

columns.title: Design

modules.title: Fundamentals
modules.blurb: Coupling, cohesion, and the one question worth asking before any change.

blocks.title: Two words that carry most of the weight
blocks.body:
Almost every design argument you will ever have reduces to two ideas, and both are about **change**, not about beauty.

### Coupling

How much one thing has to know about another. High coupling means a change over here forces a change over there. You feel it as *"I only wanted to rename a field and now forty files are red."*

### Cohesion

How much the things inside one unit actually belong together. Low cohesion means a module is a junk drawer. You feel it as *"where would I even put this?"*

The goal is **low coupling, high cohesion**, and the reason is not aesthetic. It is that software is read and modified far more often than it is written, and both properties are really predictions about how expensive the next change will be.

### The question worth asking

Before any non-trivial change:

> If this decision turns out to be wrong, how expensive is it to reverse?

Cheap-to-reverse decisions should be made quickly, by whoever is closest to the work. Expensive-to-reverse decisions deserve a conversation, a written rationale, and usually a smaller first step.

Most teams get this exactly backwards: they debate the reversible things at length and make the irreversible ones by accident.

blocks.title: Dependencies point inward
blocks.alt: Four stacked layers, interface, application, domain and infrastructure, with arrows from each of the outer layers pointing inward to the domain layer.
blocks.caption: The domain depends on nothing. Everything else plugs into it.

blocks.title: The most expensive kind of coupling is invisible
blocks.body: Two services that share a database table are coupled just as tightly as two classes that share a field, but nothing in either codebase says so. Coupling you cannot see is coupling nobody maintains.

quiz.title: Design I check
quiz.intro: Five questions. You need 80% to unlock Design II.

questions.prompt: A change to one module repeatedly forces changes in three unrelated modules. Which property is the problem?
questions.explanation: Coupling is how much one unit must know about another. Change rippling outward is its signature symptom.

questions.prompt: Which of these are signs of LOW cohesion in a module? Select every one that applies.

choices.text: Nobody can describe what it does in one sentence
Its functions share no data and call each other rarely
It has a large number of unit tests

questions.explanation: Test count says nothing about cohesion. The other three are the classic junk-drawer tells.

questions.prompt: Two microservices that read and write the same database table are loosely coupled, because they communicate over the network rather than by direct function calls.
questions.explanation: A shared schema is tight coupling with none of the visibility. Either service can break the other with a migration, and no code in either one declares the dependency.

questions.prompt: In the layered diagram from this module, which layer depends on nothing else?
questions.imageAlt: The four-layer diagram: interface, application, domain and infrastructure.
questions.explanation: The domain holds rules that would be true on paper. Everything else points inward at it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank. The goal is low coupling and high ________.
questions.explanation: Low coupling, high cohesion. Both are predictions about the cost of the next change.

modules.title: Boundaries
modules.blurb: Where to draw the lines, and why most teams draw them by org chart instead of by change pattern.

blocks.title: Draw boundaries where change happens
blocks.body:
A boundary is worth its cost when the things on either side of it **change for different reasons, at different rates, driven by different people**. That is the whole test.

Boundaries drawn for other reasons tend to fail:

- **By layer** (all controllers here, all models there) puts every real feature across every boundary.
- **By team** encodes today's org chart into tomorrow's architecture. Teams reorganise; the seams do not.
- **By technology** splits things that change together and joins things that do not.

When you get it right, most changes stay inside one boundary. When you get it wrong, every feature is a cross-cutting migration, and you will feel it in the pull request size long before you feel it in the architecture diagram.

blocks.title: A cheap diagnostic
blocks.body: Look at your last twenty merged pull requests. How many touched more than one module? If most of them did, your boundaries are not where your change is.

questions.prompt: What is the best test of whether a boundary belongs where you drew it?

choices.text: The two sides change for different reasons and at different rates
The two sides are owned by different teams
The two sides use different languages or frameworks
The two sides are roughly the same size

questions.explanation: Rate and reason of change. Everything else is a proxy that goes stale.

questions.prompt: If most of your pull requests touch several modules at once, that is evidence your boundaries are in the wrong place.
questions.explanation: Good boundaries keep the common change inside one of them.

modules.title: Trade-offs
modules.blurb: There is no best design, only a design that is honest about what it gave up.

blocks.title: Name the thing you gave up
blocks.body:
Every design decision buys something and pays for it somewhere else. A design document that lists only benefits is not a design document, it is a sales pitch.

The useful format is short:

1. **The decision.** One sentence.
2. **What it buys.** Be specific and, where possible, numeric.
3. **What it costs.** The part people skip.
4. **What would make this wrong.** The condition under which you would revisit it.

That fourth item is what separates a decision from an opinion. If you cannot describe the world in which your choice is wrong, you have not made a choice, you have made an assumption.

modules.title: Systems
modules.blurb: Scaling the same instincts up to something several teams work in at once.

blocks.title: The design problem changes shape
blocks.body:
At the system level the hard part stops being the code and starts being **agreement**. The questions that matter are about contracts, ownership and failure:

- Who owns this data, and who is merely allowed to read it?
- What is the contract, and how does it change without a synchronised deploy?
- What happens when this dependency is slow rather than down? Slow is worse.
- What is the blast radius when it fails, and who finds out first?

Notice that none of those are answered by a diagram of boxes and arrows, which is why most architecture diagrams are decoration.

columns.title: Code Craft
columns.blurb: Writing code the next person can safely change.

modules.title: Readability
modules.blurb: Naming, shape, and writing for the person who arrives after you have left.

blocks.title: Optimise for the reader
blocks.body:
Code is read far more than it is written, and almost always by someone with less context than the author had. Two habits carry most of the benefit:

**Name for intent, not for mechanism.** `retryableUsers` says why the list exists. `filteredList2` says only that somebody called filter twice.

**Make the shape match the logic.** If a function has an early bail-out, put it first and return. Deep nesting is usually a sign that several decisions are tangled into one block.

Comments should explain **why**, never **what**. The code already says what. A comment that restates the line above it is a maintenance liability, because it can go stale while the code stays correct.

blocks.title: Building a website to scale
blocks.caption: Embedded through the generic video block rather than the YouTube block, which is how you attach any iframe-based player.

blocks.title: The comment that lies
blocks.body: A wrong comment is worse than no comment. It is believed, and unlike wrong code it never throws an error.

questions.prompt: What should a code comment usually explain?

choices.text: Why the code does what it does

questions.explanation: The code states what. Only a human can state why, and only a human will miss it later.

questions.prompt: One word: a wrong comment is worse than no comment because it is still ________.
questions.explanation: Unlike wrong code, a wrong comment never fails a test.

modules.title: Review
modules.blurb: Reviewing for correctness and design without turning it into a taste fight.

blocks.title: Review against intent
blocks.body:
The single biggest improvement most teams can make to review is to **separate blocking concerns from preferences, and say which is which**. "This will break when the list is empty" and "I would have named this differently" are not the same comment, and treating them as the same is how review becomes something people dread.

The second biggest improvement is smaller pull requests. Review quality falls off sharply past a few hundred lines; past a thousand, an approval mostly means the reviewer got tired.

blocks.title: The checklist from Design I, again

modules.title: Refactoring
modules.blurb: Changing structure without changing behaviour, and knowing which one you are doing.

blocks.title: One hat at a time
blocks.body:
Refactoring means changing the structure of code **without changing its behaviour**. Adding a feature means changing behaviour. Doing both in one commit means neither the tests nor the reviewer can tell you whether you succeeded.

Swap hats deliberately: refactor, commit, then build. When a review comment says "this diff does two things", this is almost always the thing it means.

modules.title: Performance
modules.blurb: Measure, then fix the thing you measured. Not the thing you assumed.

blocks.title: The order that actually works
blocks.body:
1. **Set a target.** "Faster" is not a target. "p95 under 300ms" is.
2. **Measure where the time goes.** Profile the real workload, not a microbenchmark of the part you find interesting.
3. **Fix the largest contributor.** Not the most annoying one.
4. **Measure again.** Roughly half of confident performance fixes make nothing faster, and some make things slower.

The most common real-world win is not a clever algorithm. It is doing the work once instead of N times, or not doing it at all.

columns.title: Testing
columns.blurb: Knowing whether it works, and continuing to know.

modules.title: Unit tests
modules.blurb: What a unit test is for, and the one question that tells you if yours is any good.

blocks.title: Would it fail?
blocks.body:
The only question that matters about a test:

> If I reverted the code this test covers, would this test fail?

If the answer is no, the test is decoration. It costs time to run and maintain and buys nothing.

Good unit tests are **fast**, **deterministic** and **independent**. Independence is the one people skip: if test B only passes when test A ran first, you do not have two tests, you have one very long one with a confusing failure message.

blocks.title: Test names are documentation
blocks.body: `throwsWhenCartIsEmpty` tells a future reader the rule. `testCart3` tells them nothing and will outlive everyone who knew what it meant.

questions.prompt: A test that passes whether or not the code under test is correct is still worth keeping, because it adds coverage.
questions.explanation: It costs maintenance and run time and catches nothing. Coverage measures lines executed, not behaviour verified.

questions.prompt: Which properties should a good unit test have?
questions.explanation: The fourth one describes an integration test at best, and a bad afternoon at worst.

modules.title: Integration
modules.blurb: Testing the seams, which is where the bugs actually live.

blocks.title: Bugs live at the boundaries
blocks.body:
Unit tests verify that each part works in isolation. Most production incidents come from parts that each worked perfectly and disagreed about something at the seam: a timezone, a null, an encoding, a retry that was not idempotent.

Integration tests are slower and flakier, so run fewer of them and choose them deliberately: test the contract, not the implementation on either side of it.

modules.title: Choosing what to test
modules.blurb: Choosing what to test so the suite stays worth running.

blocks.title: Test behaviour, not structure
blocks.body:
A suite coupled to internal structure breaks on every refactor, which teaches the team that failing tests are noise. That lesson, once learned, is very expensive to unlearn.

Test through the interface a caller actually uses. Then a refactor that preserves behaviour keeps the suite green, which is exactly the signal you wanted it to give.

modules.title: In production
modules.blurb: Because some conditions only exist there.

blocks.title: Not a euphemism for being reckless
blocks.body:
Some properties cannot be observed anywhere else: real traffic shape, real data skew, real third-party latency, real concurrency. Pretending otherwise does not make staging representative.

The practices that make it responsible rather than reckless are all about **limiting blast radius and shortening the feedback loop**: feature flags, canary releases, real monitoring with alerts someone actually receives, and a rollback that has been tested more recently than the deploy.

columns.title: Delivery
columns.blurb: Getting it in front of users, and keeping it there.

modules.title: Version control
modules.blurb: A commit history is a communication medium, not a save button.

blocks.title: Write history for the reader
blocks.body:
Someone will read this history during an incident, at speed, under stress, probably a year from now, quite possibly you.

- One logical change per commit. A commit that does two things cannot be reverted cleanly.
- The subject line says **what changed**; the body says **why**.
- "fix", "wip" and "asdf" are all the same message: *I did not expect anyone to read this*.

`git bisect` is the strongest argument for small commits ever made, and it only works if each commit builds.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the body of a commit message?
questions.explanation: The diff already shows what. Only the author can record why.

modules.title: Continuous integration
modules.blurb: Merging often enough that integration stops being an event.

blocks.title: The point is the frequency
blocks.body:
Continuous integration is not "we have a build server". It is the practice of merging to the mainline often enough that conflicts stay small and integration stops being a phase of the project.

A build server that runs on a branch nobody merges for three weeks is not CI. It is a very thorough way of finding out you were wrong three weeks ago.

The non-negotiable part: **a red build is the team's top priority**. A pipeline that is normally red is a pipeline nobody reads.

modules.title: Deployment
modules.blurb: Making releases boring on purpose.

blocks.title: Boring is the goal
blocks.body:
The measure of a deployment process is not how sophisticated it is, it is how uneventful. Signals that it is working:

- Anyone on the team can do it, including on their first week.
- It happens during working hours, because it does not need heroics.
- Rolling back is a normal action with a known duration, not an incident.
- Nobody watches a dashboard holding their breath, because alerts would tell them.

Deploying and releasing are separate: ship the code dark, then turn it on. That single split removes most of the drama.

modules.title: Operations
modules.blurb: Owning it after it ships, which is where you learn what you actually built.

blocks.title: You learn the system by operating it
blocks.body:
Design tells you what the system should do. Operating it tells you what it does.

Instrument for the questions you will have at 3am, not the ones you have now: is it up, is it slow, for whom, since when, and what changed. Alert on **symptoms users feel**, not on causes you happen to be able to measure, or the alert channel becomes noise and the real page gets missed.

Run blameless post-incident reviews. An incident caused by one person's mistake is really a system that permitted that mistake, and only one of those two is worth fixing.

blocks.title: Full circle
blocks.body: Everything you learn operating a system is design feedback. That is why this column sits alongside Design rather than after it.
